In 'Suffs,' the message of this thrilling new musical is resoundingly clear
Suffs provide a split portrait of two moments in time.
Taub's score is ambitious and sweeping, with moments of genuine beauty and power, particularly in the ensemble numbers that showcase the collective strength of the suffrage movement.
It’s genuinely tuneful and effective at organizing strong characters around a complex series of events.

The strains of something less than triumphant were always lurking in Hamilton, which begins with a fist-pump to the sky but ends with the plaintive question, “Who lives, who dies, who tells your story?” But just as young Alice had no time for sweetness, Suffs has no time for wistfulness as it nears its ending.

Forget the world stage, what about Broadway? This is the route that Hillary Clinton has taken as the co-producer, with Malala Yousafzai, of Suffs, a thundering new musical by the singer and composer Shaina Taub about the American women’s suffrage movement.
But this unapologetic love letter to those who risked life and limb to get women a seat at the table is also heart-tugging, vibrant and charming.
Suffs is a full-throated musical call to action, and its message is neither subtle nor ambivalent: It wants to light a fire under you.
Suffs largely succeeds in showcasing the accomplishments of its creators and performers, particularly with regard to Ms. Taub's rich and often rousing score and the terrific cast.
“Suffs” on Broadway is vastly improved.
What “Suffs” does capture is the excitement and urgency of being swept up in the fight for a just cause, and discovering yourself and your peers in the process.

That’s not entirely inaccurate: The historical figures in the way of the likes of Alice Paul (Taub), Carrie Catt (Jen Colella) and Ida B. Wells (Nikki M. James) are buffoonish paper tigers devoid of argument or veracity....
Shaina Taub's musical about the women's suffrage movement is an ambitious and often stirring work that brings passion and intelligence to an important chapter in American history.
Still, while never less than likable, “Suffs” comes short of being riveting.
Aside from all that, dramatically speaking, it’s just that good!
Taub's masterwork—and her first musical to reach Broadway—was initially staged two Aprils back at the Public Theater.
The musical has memorable music, star-making performances, and an inspiring message with moments that tug at the heartstrings.
Taub (book, lyrics and music) has taken this weighty subject, one full of passion, sadness and personal sacrifice, and has fashioned a theater work that deftly balances history and entertainment.
“Suffs” entertains because Taub makes her show all about the women, and she makes those women committed but very flawed individuals.
In case the fire in your belly has gone out, “Suffs” will throw some coal on it.
Indeed, Taub has a unique and accomplished gift for melody and lyrics that makes you want to hear more of her work.
Winning the vote feels inevitable throughout, so without deep emotional stakes to drive the story, Suffs can feel plodding as it hits the historical beats.
Suffs is a flawed work that fails to emotionally grab, but succeeds as a fresh reminder of the necessity and power of sustained political action.
Unfortunately, there is too much plotting to sustain the show, which has enough to shoulder to make the point that the battle for equality in all arenas is never a fait accompli.
That’s a fitting message — progress comes only through perseverance — for a remarkable musical that educates and entertains.
Suffs reminds us that, as important as individual convictions and rights are, when we can agree on enough to unite side-by-side, we can change the world.
Suffs is the musical I needed as a little girl and the musical we need today.
Suffs is a winner, with a wonderful mixture of earnest storytelling, humor, and heart.

cn.t: Critics praise Shaina Taub's ambitious, tuneful musical about the suffrage movement as earnest and entertaining, though some find it more civics lesson than fully realized art. Strong performances and rousing score elevate the historical storytelling.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
